idiom_name: OwnedAttribute / OwnsOne with relational table splitting
implementation_notes: EF Core realizes Embedded Value as an owned entity type: the value is declared with [Owned] or configured with OwnsOne in OnModelCreating, and on a relational provider it is mapped to the same table as the owner - table splitting - with columns named Navigation_Property (ShippingAddress_Line1, ShippingAddress_City). The value gets a shadow primary key equal to the owner's, so no key property is needed. Owned types are still entity types underneath: they have a hidden key and reference semantics, which is why EF Core's own guidance now points value objects at complex types instead; keep owned types when the contained type must have navigations to other entities or its own table.
pitfalls: Owned types have a hidden key and reference semantics: assigning the same instance to two owned properties fails at SaveChanges, and two owned instances are never equal by value.
The same value type used twice in one owner needs distinct defining navigations plus explicit column names, otherwise EF maps both occurrences onto the same columns.
Owned reference types can only be null when mapped to their own table (older EF Core versions), so 'no address' has to be modelled deliberately.

variants.name: EF Core complex type (ComplexProperty / [ComplexType])
variants.implementation_notes: Complex types were added to EF Core precisely for value objects: no identity, no hidden key, compared by value, copied on assignment, and still mapped inline as columns of the containing entity's table (or as JSON). Microsoft's documentation states that users modelling value objects with table splitting should consider switching from owned types to complex types, because the value semantics remove the accidental-sharing and identity pitfalls. Use this whenever the value really is identity-less; use owned types when the contained type must navigate to other entities, which complex types cannot do.
pitfalls: Complex types are not discovered by convention: without [ComplexType] or ComplexProperty the type is simply not mapped, and the property is treated as an unmapped CLR property.
A mutable reference-type complex value can be shared by two properties, so mutating one changes the other; model it as a record or struct so assignment copies.
Complex types cannot contain navigations to entities - if the value needs one, it is not a value object for EF Core's purposes.
